rows.description: A child says a project will be quick and starts the night before. He imagines the ideal path and forgets past delays.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager plans to revise the whole syllabus in a weekend and feels shocked when it takes far longer. Past experience is ignored for a bright hopeful picture.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A student underestimates a thesis, a move or an application, then panics near the deadline. Tasks usually take longer than the best-case story suggests.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A mature worker checks how long similar tasks actually took, adds a buffer, and breaks the job into small parts before promising dates.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A lead sees teammates repeatedly give optimistic dates and treats it as a pattern of human thinking, not laziness, by asking for ranges and reviewing past accuracy.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A teenager sees toppers and celebrities who dropped out and succeeded and concludes the path is easy, never seeing the many who tried and quietly failed.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A student copies habits of famous founders without noticing that many people with the same habits failed. The visible sample is not the whole picture.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A thoughtful person asks where the failures are and what the whole group looked like before praising a method, course or strategy.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young professional hears that old buildings or old habits were better made, and notes that only the durable ones remain to be seen. The weaker ones are gone.

rows.description: A child wants the toy or game everyone has and changes his taste to match the group. Being included matters more than whether he likes it.
